items.title: Housing Affordability Could Unite a Divided Washington – CRE Daily
items.description: NMHC and RETTC say Democrats have won both chambers, producing divided government, and argue housing costs are the issue candidates in both parties campaigned on. About 20% of the 120th Congress will be new, which the groups see as a chance to educate lawmakers on supply, permitting and technology that can cut costs. The apartment industry wants Congress to build on the ROAD to Housing Act and favors a balanced approach to affordability measures that avoids driving up costs. Key Takeaways Apartment industry leaders say housing affordability is the issue most likely to unite Washington after the midterms, according to a post from the National Multifamily Housing Council. NMHC President Sharon Wilson Géno and Kevin Donnelly, executive director and chief advocacy officer of its RETTC affiliate, wrote that Democrats have taken both chambers of Congress, with some races still being counted. One in five members of the 120th Congress will be new. This gives the industry a chance to explain how federal policy can expand housing. Practical Over Sweeping A divided Washington favors practical, evidence-based bills over sweeping proposals, the authors argued. For example, they pointed to easing construction barriers and using technology to improve operating efficiency. They also urged lawmakers to build on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. As we covered, home building costs are rising across materials, labor, borrowing and regulation. Bill Ackman says work on releasing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could now begin. See our coverage of his comments . Why It Matters Operators will closely watch how the new Congress handles consumer-protection issues. The groups warned against overly broad demands for "corporate accountability." Instead, they favor balanced measures that protect residents and support innovation without driving up rental costs. NMHC wants to shape those discussions early. Its priorities also align with developers seeking faster permitting and fewer cost mandates. What's Next Housing supply, permitting and rental pricing technology could feature in early committee agendas. Ultimately, final midterm tallies will determine the exact margins in each chamber.

items.title: Where Developers Are Trying To Lease Public Lands To Build Data Centers
items.description: More than a dozen huge pieces of public land may soon be part of the United States’ arsenal in the global race for artificial intelligence supremacy. The Bureau of Land Management and the Department of Energy are considering leasing at least 17 public land parcels totaling 19,200 acres to developers that plan to build data centers and power infrastructure on the land, a Bisnow analysis of public records found. Just two companies are responsible for more than half of the filings. “This is a new strategy by the Trump administration,” said Chinonso Anozie, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center. “What it would do is remove a lot of local opposition and local vetoes over some of these data centers, limiting what states and local communities can also do in challenging and stopping data centers.” Flickr/Bureau of Land Management The Morley Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey National Conservation Area in Idaho, where the Bureau of Land Management is considering leasing a parcel of public land for a data center development Bisnow verified 17 proposed projects with the BLM and DOE that are either approved or pending authorization by cross-referencing federal agency records and press releases with data center trackers from two conservation and public lands advocacy groups: the Center for Western Priorities and More Than Just Parks . The majority of those projects, excluding separate land parcels for power stations, are in the western U.S., while a smattering of sites are in the Southeast. The filings show that developers are jumping on the opportunity to lease public lands, catalyzed by a July 2025 White House initiative to accelerate the country’s AI industry and by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act . Using public lands also means the federal government can flex the supremacy clause, a constitutional provision that gives federal law priority over some state laws . This tool could help developers skirt a broad cultural pushback against data centers. Industry advocacy group Data Center Coalition praised the Trump administration and the DOE for the policy initiative. “The digital infrastructure that data centers provide is essential to advancing America’s global economic competitiveness, safeguarding national security, and maintaining the country’s edge in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and many other 21st-century technologies,” Michele Nellenbach, the trade group’s vice president of federal affairs, said in a statement. But elected officials are already speaking out against leasing public lands for data center development in Idaho and Kentucky. A lack of local support could still hamper proposals far away from towns and cities, said John Boyd Jr., principal at site selection firm The Boyd Co. “Companies routinely look for some type of public-private partnership, whether that be sales tax abatements for the server equipment or property tax abatements,” Boyd said. “All of that requires county, city or state support.” Most of the companies that filed prelease applications with the BLM or have been selected for projects on DOE land didn't respond to Bisnow ’s requests for comment. SB Energy In Ohio Part of a former uranium enrichment plant near the 2,200-person town of Piketon in southern Ohio is planned to become the world’s largest data center to date. SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, broke ground on the 189-acre project in March and committed to building 10 gigawatts of new power generation connecting to the local grid. It expects to generate 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent jobs in the region. Known as the Portsmouth Site, it includes Department of Energy land. It is split between public land and some private land, according to a spokesperson for SB Energy. Flickr/U.S. Department of Energy Excavation of the Portsmouth site in 2012 as part of soil remediation efforts at the former uranium enrichment plant Valar Atomics In Utah Valar Atomics, a company focused on scaling nuclear energy for heavy industrial power, filed an application with BLM to build a 9,000-acre facility in Carbon County, Utah, NPR reported in September . BLM records confirm the filing but don't contain the project's acreage. The development, named Project Beehive, is planned to include data centers along with 456 small nuclear reactors and space to produce nuclear fuel and store nuclear waste on a Department of Energy site. A Brookfield Partnership In Kentucky A partnership between Brookfield, NextEra Energy Resources, Big Rivers Electric Corp., Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System is planning an energy generation and AI campus on a 785-acre DOE site. Construction is expected to conclude on the former Superfund site in 2031, following remediation efforts that are needed because of the site’s decades of uranium enrichment operations, according to a release from the department. A spokesperson for the Paducah American Energy Hub told Bisnow in a statement that the team is “committed to working with all stakeholders.” “We have met with many local and state officials and look forward to engaging constructively with them and the community as a whole,” the spokesperson said. But Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico in August that the Trump administration excluded him from conversations about the $100B data center project and indicated a willingness to block or delay data centers from opening. While Beshear can’t stop the data center from happening, Anozie said, local governments can still make it difficult for projects to operate once they are built. “Where the states might have a way of regulating what is going on is using state environmental laws to challenge and to say, ‘Well, you didn't get the permit for this,’” he said. “But they cannot outrightly veto or zone out that area for a data center.” Amentum And DC Blox In South Carolina The Savannah River Site was one of 16 sites identified by the DOE in April 2025 to support the construction of data centers and the

items.title: Your technology wish list is only half the story
items.description: Every mortgage technology company keeps a list of lender feature requests. Most treat it as a roadmap. That habit is one reason lenders keep buying technology, even as the cost to originate a loan remains stubbornly high. I have sat on both sides of that list. Early in my career, I was the lender buying and running point-of-sale systems, loan origination systems and CRMs. Later, I built customer success teams for lenders like the one I used to be. A feature request is a lender’s best guess at a solution. The real problem lies beneath it, and a technology partner that only builds to the request leaves that problem in place. Here is my advice to lenders, from someone who now runs a technology company: Don’t stop at the wish list. Send the why along with it. Tell your technology partners what you’re trying to accomplish, and judge them by what they do next. Not every list is the same. Some items are requirements, such as a compliance rule , an investor guideline or a business process the technology must support. Any provider worth hiring should be flexible enough to handle those. Others are feature requests, usually tweaks to something that already exists. Then there’s the wish list: new ideas about what the technology could do. Wish lists are among the most valuable inputs a technology partner can receive. They just aren’t the whole story without the reason behind them. A request is an answer, not a question Say your team asks its technology partner for a new field on the application. One provider adds the field and checks the box. Another asks why and learns you’re launching a new loan product. That provider adds the questions, then builds in logic so borrowers are prompted to upload the right documents based on their answers. Same request, very different result. The difference is context. Not every lender wants that conversation every time, and that’s fair. If you’re hungry and order a salad, you may not want the server asking why. Sometimes you just need the field. But when a request is tied to something bigger, such as a new product, a new market or a change in how loans move through your shop, a few extra minutes on the why can save a lot of rework later. The best technology partners ask bigger questions than “What do you want from your point of sale?” What do you expect from the industry over the next few years? Which loan products matter most to your growth? What should borrowers experience at each step? How are your loans performing after they close? A partner that asks those questions is building for your business. One that only collects feature lists is building for its backlog. Put context back into the RFP The same dynamic shows up when lenders buy technology. For many banks, credit unions and larger lenders, a formal request for proposal (RFP) is required, and for good reason: Single-source procurement is bad practice. The RFP isn’t the issue. The format often is. A spreadsheet passed around without context and scored with checkmarks rewards the provider willing to say yes to every line. It reveals little about whether that provider understands how a loan moves from application to servicing, or whether it will still ship useful work two years after the contract is signed. Lenders can maintain rigor and add context. Pair the spreadsheet with live working sessions, share the business goals behind the requirements and ask finalists how they would solve the problem behind a line item, not just whether they can check it. A point-of-sale decision touches processing, underwriting , closing, secondary marketing and servicing. Choices made in the first minutes of an application ripple through the loan’s entire life. A provider that only sees its own screen will optimize that screen. Watch what partners build without being asked Shipping on a regular schedule is the bare minimum. What I look for in a partner, and what lenders should expect from us, is a release that solves a problem in a way the lender didn’t picture or never thought to request. You know you’ve seen one when the lender’s first reaction is some version of, “Wait, why didn’t we have this already?” Getting there means a technology company has to say no to some requests. If you build whatever gets the most votes, you end up with a product designed for the average lender. I’ve never met a lender who thinks of themselves as average. Cost is the honest scorecard Cost is the pressure every lender feels most. In the second quarter of 2026, independent mortgage banks and bank-owned mortgage companies spent $10,936 to produce each loan, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association . The average, dating back to the second quarter of 2008, is $7,945. Automation should take repetitive work off the desks of loan officers, processors and underwriters, not replace them, so those people can spend their time on judgment, problem-solving and the borrower relationships that build a business. Every technology company claims to deliver that. Few can prove it. Make them show you. Before you sign anything, have the provider take a real loan file from application to closing and point to the specific steps its technology took off someone’s plate. If they can’t walk you through those steps, I’d be skeptical of any savings they’re promising. Borrowers still retype what they already uploaded Around 2016, one of the first things I did in that IT role was map the lender’s borrower journey. Many of our borrowers came through real estate agents. Imagine a couple finding their dream home online, with professionally shot photos that make everything feel possible. Then they go to apply for a mortgage and are sent back decades in time to a confusing PDF. Should they print it? Can they type into it? Do they check the box or circle it? Didn’t they already provide this information? A decade later, point-of-sale technology is standard, and no one is going back to that PDF. items.title: Mapped: Where the Most Homeowners Own Their Homes Outright With No Mortgage
items.description: Roughly 3 in 5 American homeowners pay a mortgage every month, yet the share of those who own their property outright is steadily growing—with at least half of all homeowners in three states now completely mortgage-free . According to a new Realtor.com® data analysis of the recently released 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates , 59% of homeowners carried a mortgage last year, while 41% owned their homes free and clear. That marks a major shift from 2010, when fewer than a third of homes (32.8%) were owned outright while 67% carried home loan debt. Mortgaged homeownership has shrunk across all four regions, though reliance on financing still varies significantly by geography. The West had the highest mortgage debt rate at 63.8%, while the South recorded the lowest at 56.8%. The Northeast and Midwest tied at 58.7%. At the state level, West Virginia led the nation with 56.6% of its homeowners living mortgage-free, followed by Mississippi (52.7%) and New Mexico (50%). On the other side of the spectrum, Washington, DC, in 2025 logged the lowest share of outright homeownership, at just 26.5%, trailed by Maryland (30.6%) and Colorado (31.6%). Loading... Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu explains that the balance between mortgaged and free-and-clear homes meaningfully shapes housing market dynamics, especially at a time when mortgage rates are high. "Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs," says Xu. "Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs." Ultimately, those market forces sway inventory levels, home prices, and whether first-time buyers can access homeownership. With mortgage rates stuck above 7% and the Federal Reserve all but certain to raise interest rates in December—and possibly again in January 2027—to combat inflation, the lock-in effect is poised to chill the market again . Homeowners sitting on low mortgage rates are reluctant to give them up, keeping much-needed inventory off the market. That supply squeeze, in turn, puts upward pressure on prices and makes it harder for renters to access homeownership. Free-and-clear owners, however, are not bound by borrowing costs and can list whenever they choose. "A mortgage-free owner isn’t watching interest rates to decide when to move," Christie Goldman , a real estate agent with Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Central in Charleston, WV , tells Realtor.com. "They can buy their next home with cash, which makes their offer stronger, and they can close on their own timeline without a lender, an appraisal contingency, or rate risk." Loading... The Mountain State leads the way Across the 50 states and the District of Columbia, West Virginia stands out with the lowest share of mortgaged homes, at 43.4%, and conversely the highest share of outright ownership, at 56.6%. Two main forces drive this dynamic: relatively low median home prices and an older population that tends to hold on to properties longer than residents in many other states. "In West Virginia, a paid-off home isn’t a someday goal. It's how people here live," says Goldman. "When people put down roots here, they stay." It is common for a local family to purchase a home, raise their children there, and pay it off, often with the next generation buying property in the same community. According to Goldman, affordability is what makes that cycle possible. In October 2026, the median asking price in West Virginia was $259,999, well below the national median of $415,000. "At those prices, owning your home free and clear is a realistic goal here, not a distant dream," says the agent, pointing to the 2025 United Van Lines’ national study that ranked West Virginia as the second-leading inbound destination for movers. "Many of those buyers sell a higher-priced home elsewhere and can pay cash here," says Goldman. "Once they discover the mountains, the community, and the pace of life, they don’t want to leave." Loading... West Virgina has the nation's highest share of homeowners who own property outright, at nearly 57%. Posnov/Getty Images Xu also attributes West Virginia's high share of mortgage-free owners to the state's slow population growth, particularly among young adults, which has kept new borrowers from entering the market in large numbers. Between 2015 and 2025, the population aged 18–34 fell 5% in West Virginia, while the same age group in the U.S. grew 3.8%. Owning one's home outright offers many perks, sharply reducing monthly expenses and creating a buffer against economic headwinds. "Mortgage-free homeowners have more financial flexibility, especially with today's higher interest rates and rising living costs," Thomas O’Shaughnessy , vice president and real estate broker at Clever Real Estate , tells Realtor.com. "They don't have monthly mortgage payments, which makes it easier to manage expenses, save money, and handle unexpected repairs or emergencies." In theory, a high percentage of debt-free homeowners can also help unlock inventory for the next wave of buyers. "They may be more willing to list, downsize, move elsewhere, or buy again," says O'Shaughnessy. "All of these can improve inventory and help move the market in your community." items.title: America’s Trillion-Dollar Credit Card Debt Threatens To Lock Millions Out of the Housing Market
items.description: With prices still alarmingly high, it comes as no surprise that Americans are increasingly turning to credit cards more than ever. But doing so could be silently sabotaging any hope of owning a home , if you’re not careful. Last week, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York published its latest household debt report . Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier, and total household debt, including mortgages, auto loans, and student loans, expanded by $334 billion for the period to a record $19.1 trillion. High levels of debt are problematic for anyone, but most especially for first-time homebuyers. If your ambitions for 2027 include buying a home, it’s important to get your debt in check before it’s too late. Easy money comes at a price According to TransUnion’s most recent quarterly credit industry insights report , the number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million up from 174.8 million. The ease of use means most people turn to credit cards for their everyday purchases, like groceries, gas, and utility bills—all of which have seen a steep increase in prices over the past two years. Now, if you’re someone who pays off their credit card in full each month, you’re in the clear. If not, the average interest rate on a new credit card offer currently stands at about 24%, and debt can accumulate quickly. And this can cause an array of issues for first-time homebuyers. "Issues arising from high levels of consumer debt are amplified for first-time homebuyers as they typically have less savings, limited financial history, and tighter financial conditions,” John Donikian , vice president of Best Interest Financial in West Bloomfield, MI , tells Realtor.com® . Loading... Credit card debt is nothing to ignore, especially if you're hoping to buy a home. Getty Images The problem with carrying too much credit card debt Firstly, carrying too much debt can negatively affect your credit score , a vital metric in getting a mortgage. While there is no firm number to qualify for a mortgage, a good credit score ranges from 700 to 749, and most conventional loans typically require at least 620. Lenders may accept lower scores if you have a larger down payment or other strong financial factors. The higher your balances are, the more your score is dragged down, which can not only affect the interest rate a lender can offer you, but also keep you from getting a mortgage with some lenders entirely. “Your credit score doesn’t just determine if you are approved; it influences your interest rate and the monthly payment you are offered,” says Jake Vehige , president of mortgage lending at Neighbors Bank. “Even a small difference in interest rates can add up to thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.” Secondly, as part of the process of getting a mortgage, lenders will look at your debt-to-income ratio to see how much house you can afford. If a lender looks at your total monthly debt payments against your gross monthly income and your DTI exceeds its caps, your application could be delayed or even denied outright. But both of those instances can be reversed, with time and a fixed budget that allows you to pay off your debt. In other words, your credit score can rebound. Where first-time buyers are really at a disadvantage by accumulating so much credit card debt is the drain it will put on their savings. The money that you’ll need to rack up to pay off the 20%-plus interest on your bills could have been money saved for your down payment, closing costs, and repair funds. Many lenders also require proof of postclosing cash reserves, which is much harder to build while paying down high-interest debt. “Ideally, you want to keep your credit card balances at no more than 20% to 30% of your maximum credit limit," explains Jeremy Schachter , branch manager at Fairway Independent Mortgage Corp. in Phoenix . "For example, if you have a $1,000 limit, don’t go over a balance higher than $200 to $300. Anything that exceeds that amount can lower your credit score and make it difficult to get approved for a mortgage with a good rate.” Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. She previously served as the managing editor at HollywoodLife.com, the executive editor at PerezHilton.com, and as a managing editor at Mediavine. Her work has also appeared on MSN, Yahoo News, and BlogHer. She is a proud graduate of Emerson College in Boston and is originally from New Jersey.

items.title: Hedge fund pressures Invitation Homes to speed up home sales
items.description: Activist investor Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressing single-family rental giant Invitation Homes to accelerate home sales, sharply increase capital returns and scale back growth plans, arguing the company’s stock trades at a steep discount to the value of its houses. In an open letter to shareholders released Monday, the Stamford, Connecticut-based hedge fund said it believes Invitation Homes is “among the most undervalued companies in the REIT sector” and criticized the board and management for what it called “complacency” and “half measures” in addressing the gap. Land & Buildings, which owns an undisclosed stake in Invitation Homes, is led by Jonathan Litt, a longtime activist in the real estate investment trust sector. Invitation Homes (NYSE: INVH) is the nation’s largest owner of single-family rental homes, with more than 80,000 properties concentrated in Sun Belt and other high-growth markets. Discount to home values at center of dispute Land & Buildings said the public market values Invitation Homes’ properties at roughly $270,000 per home, compared with an average sale price of about $460,000 on homes the company has sold since December 2025. That implies a discount of about 40%, according to the letter, which was disseminated via GlobeNewswire. The firm said it separately valued more than 90% of the company’s wholly owned portfolio, “address by address,” and arrived at an estimated average value of approximately $425,000 per home. Something has to give,” the firm said in the letter. Years of underperformance versus peers Land & Buildings also highlighted what it described as sustained underperformance. Over the past three years, Invitation Homes ranks second to last in that compensation peer group, trailing the group average by more than 35 percentage points, according to Land & Buildings. Shareholders who held the stock for five years have lost more than 20% of their investment, including dividends, the letter said, even as U.S. home prices have continued to climb. The firm noted that Invitation Homes’ shares now trade at an implied capitalization rate of about 7%, roughly 60 basis points wider than American Homes 4 Rent, and at a lower multiple of adjusted funds from operations. The letter also pointed to legal and regulatory costs. Land & Buildings said Invitation Homes has paid more than $79 million to resolve four legal matters related to resident treatment and business practices, including a $48 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024. At the same time, the board approved more than $25 million in special retention awards in March 2026 for the CEO and three other executives, according to the firm. “This troubling misalignment and lack of accountability is deeply concerning,” Land & Buildings said. Capital could be returned through share repurchases or special dividends for as long as the stock trades below estimated NAV. Offer renters a path to homeownership. items.title: Villa hires former Century Communities CFO Messenger as CEO
items.description: Villa , a San Francisco-based manufactured homebuilder, has appointed homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO, the company announced on Monday. Founded in 2019, Villa says it has delivered more than 425 homes using an offsite construction model that spans accessory dwelling units (ADUs), multifamily projects and new neighborhoods. The company manages feasibility, design, permitting, site preparation and installation, and partners with a network of factories for production, according to the announcement. Messenger brings decades of financial and operating experience in homebuilding and multifamily real estate, having spent more than 10 years as chief financial officer of Century Communities . During his tenure, Century expanded from about 150 to 1,800 employees across 18 states, grew to $4.5 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,000 annual closings, completed seven acquisitions and raised more than $3 billion in debt and equity capital, the company said. He also led Century’s initial public offering and helped launch its mortgage, title and insurance subsidiaries, giving him direct experience with the vertically integrated models many large homebuilders use to manage costs and capture more of the housing value chain. Earlier in his career, Messenger spent roughly a decade at UDR , a publicly traded multifamily real estate investment trust, where he advanced through senior finance roles to become CFO. Messenger’s appointment comes as Villa looks to expand beyond individual ADUs and small projects into larger communities in partnership with land developers and homebuilders. The company is already working on new neighborhoods including the 25-home Acacia Village in Santa Rosa, California, Alpine Village in Westminster, Colorado, and homes in Altadena, California, for families rebuilding after the Eaton Fire, according to the release. Investors say his background in scaling a public homebuilder and in capital markets was a key factor in the decision. “Villa has demonstrated its capabilities across ADUs, multifamily properties and new neighborhoods, and Dave is the right leader to build on Villa’s success and advance its growth strategy,” said Aaron Marsh, partner and CFO at Unless, an investor in Villa and member of Villa’s board of directors. “He brings deep housing experience, a track record of scaling businesses nationally and a clear understanding of what land and development partners need to move projects forward.” Messenger said he sees an opportunity to apply processes from large-scale homebuilding to Villa’s offsite platform. “This team has done what much of our industry has only talked about: delivering quality homes through offsite construction across individual properties, multifamily communities and new neighborhoods,” Messenger said in the announcement. “I see great potential to build on that foundation by bringing a large-scale homebuilder’s operating discipline to Villa, with an emphasis on predictable execution and profitable growth.” Villa’s model aims to give homeowners, multifamily operators and developers a single partner from concept through completion. The company handles site feasibility, site and home design, permitting and on-site work and uses factory partners to build homes offsite, aiming for more predictable timelines and costs than traditional stick-built construction, according to the release. “Dave has an exceptional track record spanning homebuilding, multifamily real estate, capital markets and land development,” said Heather Miksch, chief operating officer at Villa. “As we build on Villa’s momentum and pursue development opportunities, his experience will be invaluable in helping us grow our business while continuing to serve both homeowners and development partners.” Related More: homebuilder Real Estate

Vidal was named president of REMAX in September, after The Real Brokerage completed its acquisition of REMAX, forming the Real REMAX Group . In an emailed statement, a REMAX spokesperson told HousingWire that the president of REMAX has always overseen the company’s Canadian operation. As Vidal moves into the Canadian leadership position, Don Kottick, who has served as the president of REMAX Canada since April 2025, has announced plans to leave the firm on Dec. 15. This information was conveyed to REMAX brokers and franchisees via an internal memo reviewed and confirmed by HousingWire. “This move helps ensure every REMAX region around the world receives as much of the same focus, momentum and opportunities as possible,” the internal memo stated. “The next few months will be pivotal as we roll out new technology and invest in further strengthening the REMAX brand in Canada and around the world.” Prior to joining REMAX, Kottick was the president and CEO of Sotheby’s International Realty Canada . Before joining REMAX, Vidal served as the president of ERA Real Estate , helping lead the brand through Compass International Holdings ’s acquisition of its parent company Anywhere Real Estate . Compass and ERA are currently suing Vidal , claiming that he violated non-compete agreements through his move to REMAX. In the legal complaint filed in mid-October, Compass claims that the non-compete agreement prevents Vidal from serving as president or providing service to any competing business for a period of one year from his departure from ERA. items.title: CCM leader Brady Mullen's playbook to win reverse mortgage referrals without a hard sales pitch
items.description: Brady Mullen, divisional business development manager for CrossCountry Mortgage (CCM), spent 20 years as a financial adviser before selling his practice in 2021. In his experience, advisers are rarely trained on how to properly handle real estate, the biggest asset owned by most of their clients. In seeking to close that gap, Mullen changed his career trajectory by moving into reverse mortgages, first at American Liberty Mortgage before his arrival at CCM in late 2024. He believes that reverse mortgages are the most misunderstood and underappreciated financial tools on the market. In his work to grow reverse mortgage originations at one of the nation's largest independent mortgage banks, Mullen has focused on helping loan officers build a steady stream of referral partners, including financial planners, real estate agents and attorneys. That task often meets resistance as referral sources can have the same stigmas about the products as consumers. At last week's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Conference & Expo and San Antonio, Mullen discussed ways to create stronger referral networks. His advice in a nutshell? Take what works and let go of the rest. Plant, nourish, harvest Mullen chooses to organize his business development efforts in similar fashion to a farmer growing crops. Planting season involves prospecting and presentations. Fertilizing and nourishing involves follow-up conversations. Harvesting is what occurs when the leads arrive. Each of the three stages includes its own subprocesses, he explained, a structure that allows a loan officer or branch manager to see where leads stall and fix the bottleneck. When interacting with a potential referral source, Mullen suggests that reverse mortgage professionals remove words like "educate" and "teach" from their vocabulary. Telling another adult that "I want to educate you" sounds condescending, he said. Instead, offer a benefit that has nothing to do with money, such as continuing education credits. "If it's structured as CE, you've set the tone to have a discussion that, by design, was created by you to go through the topics in the order that you want and to deliver them with the visuals," Mullen said. Mullen told the NRMLA audience that advice on money-making activities should not be part of referral partner conversations. Other professionals know how to make money, he said, and people who have misconceptions about the product are likely to be turned off by the phrase, "Here's how I can help you make money." Instead, frame the discussion around providing answers. A financial adviser's clients, for example, may want to know how they can help their parents or grandparents. "You're not trying to sell reverse mortgages. You're not trying to get a referral. What are you trying to get? A presentation. … That's all you want. Don't ask for more because you'll spoil the opportunity," he explained. Validate, inform, call to action Once the seeds have been planted and a referral partner has agreed to learn more, reverse mortgages professionals should create an arc with their presentations. The first step is validation, as referrals partners won't recommend something they won't use themselves. With Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), emphasize the built-in protections of mortgage insurance premiums . Someone clinging to the idea that reverse mortgages are scams needs to know about their robust regulations through the Federal Housing Administration and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau . He also calls for simplified language. Describe the HECM product as an expanding line of credit and avoid creating confusion by explaining principal limit factors. Outline the key features that define every reverse mortgage — optional monthly payments , no balloon payments and nonrecourse provisions. From there, give a clear explanation of the financial benefits for borrowers. He used the example of a $300,000 loan at a 7% rate. A forward mortgage that amortizes over 15 years costs roughly $2,700 a month, while a 30-year loan costs about $2,000 a month. Interest-only options may only trim a few hundred dollars per month. But reverse mortgages do not require a payment and can be more efficient in terms of opportunity costs. For instance, a 75-year-old couple can take $50,000 out of a retirement account or they can borrow it, but their net worth is still the same. Borrowing offers the potential added benefits of tax savings and asset control. "Your balance sheet doesn't care whether it's paying an opportunity cost or interest. It treats them indifferently. It's going to reflect both of those equally," Mullen said. "If we're not looking at the other side of the balance sheet, we're missing half the picture, and that's a lot of picture for an expert to miss." For the right type of referral relationship, Mullen believes that longer educational videos, rather than shorter sound bites, are more helpful. He said his most popular YouTube video on reverse mortgages is 43 minutes long. When assigned as homework before a meeting, this type of content allows the referral partner to fully absorb the concepts and share them with clients, who can potentially screen themselves out without further time and energy spent by the LO. To properly nurture these relationships, Mullen says to contact them every two to three weeks. Don't worry if people unsubscribe from marketing campaigns , since this will allow you to focus on engaged prospects. "Would you rather have a distribution list of 1,000 and very little engagement, or a distribution list of 80 and have a lot of engagement? The second is by far more effective," Mullen said. items.title: Dutch Rental System Change Will Help Income But Won't Stop Home Decline
items.description: Changes to the Dutch housing rental system devised to give private landlords more financial breathing room are unlikely to stem the drop in private rental supply, according to Savills. From Jan. 1, 2027, adjustments to the rental points system — woningwaarderingsstelsel, or WWS — will let landlords of certain regulated homes charge higher rents while the homes stay regulated. The changes target homes affected by the cap on official property value (WOZ), self-contained homes without outdoor space, small listed homes in monumental buildings and homes with a very low WOZ value. Pexels/Jan van der Wolf The new WOZ-based surcharge could tack on several hundred euros of rent for certain midrange assets in cities with higher property value, but it will not stop the decline in private rental supply or reset the market, Savills said in its latest Spotlight report . The private rental stock shrank by about 22,000 homes in the year to Jan. 1, 2026, according to Statistics Netherlands , as private individuals’ rental holdings fell by nearly 37,000. The rental point system in the Netherlands scores a home on features such as floor space, energy label and property value. The total determines the maximum legal rent. In 2026, homes with up to 143 points count as social housing, with rent capped at €933 a month. Those with 144 to 186 points are regulated midrent, capped at €1,228. Above 186 points, a home is in the free-rental sector, with no maximum rent. How much landlords stand to gain depends on how much the WOZ cap currently limits the rent. In Savills’ example from its report, a fictitious Amsterdam apartment valued at €600K could command an extra €92 a month. The firm’s calculations put the surcharge at €28 to €310 a month and predict the impact to be greatest in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht, and in other areas with high property values. Former rental homes sold were found to be the most valuable ones, according to Statistics Netherlands. Properties that became owner-occupied had an average WOZ value of €375K, against €327K for all homes let by private landlords. The change was most evident in the G4 cities, where 11% to 15% of individuals’ rental homes moved to the owner-occupied sector over 2024 and 2025. “The adjustment gives landlords of selected homes more rental headroom, but does not fundamentally change the market,” Quint Luiken, commercial manager for asset and property management at Savills, said in a statement. In addition to adjustments to the WWS, the government also wants to extend a 10% rent premium for newly built midrent homes. The premium currently applies to projects that start construction before 2028. The proposal, which has yet to be approved, would push the deadline to Jan. 1, 2032. items.title: Corum Buys Dublin Office And Industrial Portfolio For €100M-Plus
items.description: Courtesy of Deloitte Real Estate Corum has invested more than €100M in its latest Irish deal. French investment manager Corum has agreed to acquire 24 properties at Dublin’s Blanchardstown Corporate Park in a deal worth more than €100M, making it one of Ireland’s largest commercial property transactions of 2026. The portfolio, acquired from Channor Real Estate Group in a deal brokered by Deloitte and Lisney , comprises approximately 370K SF of Grade A office and light industrial accommodation. Blanchardstown Corporate Park has been developed and managed by Channor over the past 30 years, and the wider 100-acre campus contains more than 1M SF of office, industrial and retail accommodation. “There was strong market interest in this portfolio of buildings because they represented a rare opportunity to acquire an established commercial development with long-term and solid commercial potential,” Deloitte Ireland Real Estate Managing Director Dessie Kilkenny said in a statement. Corum AM partner Jonny Smith added that the acquisition would broaden the fund's industrial exposure. “This transaction demonstrates the fund’s continued growth and its ability to acquire sizeable portfolios that offer opportunities across the risk spectrum and broaden its industrial exposure. Transactions of this kind will remain central to the fund’s strategy as it pursues pan-European and transatlantic opportunities,” Smith said in a statement. Blanchardstown Corporate Park was established by the Harrison family in 1996 and is home to more than 200 Irish and international businesses. Recent lettings include a 30,500 SF facility to electrical infrastructure manufacturer Hager, which is using the property as its new Irish headquarters. Channor Real Estate Group CEO Darren Harrison said the deal marked a milestone for the company after three decades developing the business park and described it as a “landmark transaction” and a "testament to the vision and commitment" that had gone into developing Blanchardstown Corporate Park. The acquisition comes as investment activity gathers pace. Investment reached €2.16B in the first nine months of 2026, up 34% on the same period last year, according to Colliers . Industrial and logistics assets attracted €164M across six transactions in the third quarter, while international investors accounted for 87% of total spending. Colliers expects full-year investment to exceed €3B, which would make 2026 the strongest year since 2022. items.title: New Firm Seeks Funds For $250M Tysons Project With Conservative Vision
items.description: A fledgling company led by a right-wing political operative is raising money for a half-million-square-foot mixed-use project in Tysons featuring a for-profit conservative institute. But it hasn’t yet picked a site or spoken to local officials about the project. And the scope of the company raises questions about whether it will be able to secure the funds to make it happen. Keyserling Management Group, founded in April, is scouting for sites for a project that is estimated to cost between $200M and $250M, the firm announced in a press release last week. Its vision includes a center “for high culture in innovation and science,” a 165-room hotel, up to 200 apartments, office, retail and restaurant space, a park, a public atrium and a chapel theater. The center, dubbed the Kayden Institute, would be designed for research and development and educational publishing and would offer classes promoting continental philosophy that has been “suppressed in modern times,” according to its website . Michael said he started a private placement offering for accredited investors, focusing on “strategic” partners. KMG has hired SVN Providence Realty Advisors to identify and evaluate sites for the proposed development. The firm has yet to reach out to Fairfax County or Tysons about the project, and at least one Fairfax County supervisor signaled opposition to the ideology behind it when asked by Bisnow . When asked what he would do if the fundraising didn’t come through, Michael said he would self-fund the institute, but likely not with the entire mixed-use development attached. Michael said the hope is to break ground by June 2028. SVN co-founder Terrell Marsh said in a separate interview that he views that timeline as aggressive, and that more realistically, shovels would be in the ground in two to two and a half years. Company’s Founding KMG was founded by Keiko "Kay" Berg in April, who died that same month, Michael said. The company was registered on April 17 with Virginia’s State Corporation Commission and lists an address in the city of Fairfax. KMG’s website lists a different address in Arlington. Underneath the Arlington address, the website misspells its email address as Info@keyerslinggroup.com. Glenn Youngkin in 2021 and advocated for President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance in the 2024 election. He told Bisnow that he was the campaign manager for Jerry Torres, the Republican congressional candidate for Virginia’s 8th District in 2024, who lost the election. Michael told Bisnow that those companies no longer have websites. items.title: Manhattan’s Top 2 Sales This Week Go Under Contract After Price Hikes
items.description: The top-two sales in Manhattan last week were in signature luxury buildings that have seen very strong sales and were able to raise their prices from initial launch. The No. 1 contract, a 17th floor unit at 1122 Madison Ave. , is pending with an ask of $38.75 million, a bit over its original ask of $38 million in January. The next highest contact, Penthouse B at The Henry on 211 W. 84th St., went under contract with an ask of $28.75 million, a hefty bump over its August 2024 price tag of $24.95 million. Both units were sponsor sales in new construction, and are full-service luxury buildings with renowned architects and designers. The buildings essentially look at each other from across Central Park, one on the upper east side, one on the upper west. "This is a sponsor strategy," says luxury broker Michael Reisor , of the Compass-affiliated Reisor.Team in Manhattan, who is familiar with both locations. "It's escalating pricing based on absorption." Loading... Manhattan's No. 2 sale this week, Penthouse B at The Henry on 211 W. 84th St., went under contract with an ask of $28.75 million, a hefty bump over its August 2024 price tag of $24.95 million Realtor.com Escalating pricing can create a sense of exigency in the buyer, offering a strong incentive not to dilly-dally with an offer, as the price will likely increase over time. "The initial release pricing will always go up as the market absorbs apartments," he says. "This gives people the urgency of, 'If we don't act now and secure the apartment, then it's just going to get more expensive.'" However, the early release strategy "doesn't always work unless buildings are this in demand," the broker says of the two top sales. The strategy is obviously successful, as the first building has only one unit left, and the second has only four. Both complexes have highly desired locations as well being architecturally significant with bold names attached: Studio Sofield for 1122 Madison Ave. and Robert A.M. Stern Architects (RAMSA) for The Henry. Nor did either development spare expense on finishes, materials, appliances, or amenities. (There is one key difference, however: The Madison Ave. building doesn't have a parking garage.) Additionally, both are boutique buildings with a controlled number of residences: 26 for the first, and 45 for the second. With buildings like this, says Reisor, there usually is no downward negotiation on pricing. "If you're selling really well, especially on a certain line, developers are always looking to maximize what they can get," agrees Manhattan broker Lisa K. Lippman of Brown Harris Stevens, who is familiar with both buildings. She says that once The Henry sold its penthouses quickly, it was off to the races in terms of price. Loading... A sprawling, full-floor new-construction luxury penthouse in Manhattan's Upper West Side has officially gone into contract off a $28.75 million asking price. Realtor.com Loading... Encompassing over 6,200 square feet of interior living space, this exclusive six-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom residence features a private vestibule, formal dining room, custom library, and an expansive private terrace with architectural setbacks. Realtor.com In February, the 1122 Madison building's penthouse duplex went under contract for $89.5 million , setting a record for a condo on the Upper East Side, and also giving leeway for the building to raise prices. Lippman, who heads up sales at another Stern building, 200 W. 88th St. , has just raised prices on its A line due to its popularity, thanks to it being a corner line with four-bedroom layouts. "We sold so many of them that we felt we could raise prices there," she says. "When a building launches and signs a significant number of contracts in a relatively short period, the sponsor may recognize that the remaining inventory is worth more than originally anticipated," agrees Michelle Griffith of Douglas Elliman, who has shown clients in both buildings. She notes that there is a strong pricing difference between new development and resale, saying, "On the resale side, it's generally less common for sellers to raise an asking price once a property is already listed." Welcome to 1122 Madison Ave. The 1122 Madison Avenue full-floor condo comes with five bedrooms, five bathrooms, two balconies, a powder room, a library, a home office, and a laundry room. Then there's the sweeping Central Park and Metropolitan Museum of Art views from the great room, library, eat-in kitchen, and primary bedroom suite. Despite being built in 2026, the building has a convincing prewar look. The unit boasts European white oak Parquet de Versailles-inspired flooring in the entrance hall and entertaining spaces, and quarter sawn European white oak plank flooring in all living areas, as well as soaring 11-foot high ceilings. The impressive amenity suite contains two floors of leisure and wellness spaces, with a squash court with a retractable basketball hoop, a fitness center programmed by The Wright Fit, a private training studio with Pilates reformer, a spa with a steam room, sauna, and cold plunge, and a sports simulator. On the lower level is a drawing room, a residents' lounge with bar, private dining room, billiard room, media room, game room, and children's playroom. All but one unit is sold out, yet the complex won't be completed until fall of 2027. Griffith says the building is doing particularly well because it's a boutique, brand-new condo in a neighborhood that is "largely defined by older co-op buildings." items.title: Unlicensed Plumber Accused of Squatting and Subleasing Rooms in Senior Woman’s Home
items.description: A California woman who hired a plumber to make repairs to her home while she was living elsewhere says he took over the property, moved strangers into the house, and locked her out—sparking a two-year nightmare that left her fighting to reclaim her own home . Jordy Smith , 76, said the man working on the plumbing at her home in San Diego's City Heights neighborhood allegedly transferred the utilities into his own name and began renting out rooms to strangers, pocketing the payments. Smith and her partner, who owned the home, later discovered the man was not a licensed plumber; but by then, the situation had spiraled out of control. When the couple returned home, they were locked out of their own house and couldn’t get the new occupants to leave, she claimed. "He just took over and, like, before we knew it, there was like 15 people," Smith told ABC 10News . "Once that happened, it really made it look like to the homeless people that were coming in, that made it look like it was his house.” The couple tried to confront the people living in the home but Smith said they had locked the door and wouldn’t talk. "I couldn't sleep at night," Smith said. "I mean, it just seemed like we'd never get back home." Meanwhile, the property had attracted multiple visits by the police. San Diego police were called to the home more than 30 times between Jan. 1, 2024, and Aug. 17, 2026, for reports of suspected drug activity, trespassing, and smoke coming from the property, according to dispatch records. In an attempt to get the squatters removed from the property, Smith turned to police and the courts for help but quickly ran into multiple roadblocks. One of the issues being that Smith’s partner couldn’t find the trust agreement that had been given to him by his mother decades before, which established ownership of the home. They ultimately listed the home for sale and reached out to the Squatter Squad, a company that helps homeowners remove unauthorized occupants. Loading... Jordy Smith, 76, said the man working on the plumbing at her home in San Diego's City Heights neighborhood allegedly transferred the utilities into his own name and began renting out rooms to strangers, pocketing the payments. Google Earth “He knew that he was the one that was the successor trustee, but they couldn't find the trust anywhere,” Kimrey Kotchick , co-founder of the Squatter Squad said, referring to Smith’s partner, who owned the property. He told 10News that squatter squatter disputes are often treated as civil matters, meaning that even when police respond to a home, if someone claims to be a renter, it is often left for the courts to resolve. Fortunately for Smith and her partner, Kotchick was able to locate the missing ownership documents through the county recorder's office. But it took another five months before the squatters could be legally evicted. After years of trying to regain access to the house, Smith and her partner were faced with another loss–the home was left in disrepair and many of Smith's cherished antiques were missing. The couple has since sold the house but Smith says the emotional toll from the ordeal has taken its toll. Now, Smith is urging other homeowners to keep their ownership documents readily accessible and think twice before leaving contractors unsupervised in their homes. items.title: Renter survey: Why fee transparency matters in AI-powered property search
items.description: Renter survey: Why fee transparency matters in AI-powered property search Published Nov. 16, 2026 By Hallie Busta Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print Permission granted by Zillow Sponsored content By Zillow Rentals SPONSORED CONTENT BY Fee transparency is quickly shifting from “nice to have” to a core differentiator for multifamily operators looking to stand out in a crowded market. New data from Zillow, based on a survey of more than 53,700 renters nationwide, found that nearly all (96%) want all fees disclosed, and more than three-quarters (78%) prefer they be bundled into their rent for a single, clear, all-in cost. Prospects wanting to know exactly how much it will cost to live at a property isn’t new, but the arrival of artificial intelligence (AI) in their searches is raising the stakes for operators to answer that question. Zillow found that 28% of recent renters who used AI anywhere in their search used it to negotiate — with this number rising to 37% among those renting in buildings with 50 or more units. AI search lets renters ask specific, plain language questions about a property, and its answers prioritize complete, accurate listings that include all the information renters want to know. “Growing cost concerns and rising AI use should be a catalyst for treating fee transparency as part of the decision experience, not just a disclosure requirement,” says Brian Miller, Principal for Industry & Partnership at Zillow Rentals. Renters’ priorities are shifting The data makes it clear: Today’s renter wants affordability and value. That means amenities and new finishes aren’t as attractive as they once were. Operators that can show how their property delivers on affordability and value (with or without the wellness rooms and bowling alleys ) are more likely to convert prospects into renters and keep them. Rising renter costs are fueling this shift: Security deposits are up roughly $200 year over year, and the share of renters paying at least 1 recurring fee other than for pets rose 11 points during that time, according to the survey data. Meanwhile, the data indicate renters are factoring in their commute and walkability more than before — unsurprising, as fuel prices remain high and volatile across the country. AI is elevating renters’ fee transparency demands AI is changing property search by letting prospects ask highly specific questions to help them decide whether your property meets their needs before they even step foot on-site. Operators should be mindful of this trend: a significant majority (78%) of recent renters used AI at least once during the searching, shopping, or renting process . Top uses for AI during property search, according to Zillow’s survey of recent renters: Home recommendations: 56% Personalized answers about their lease: 45% (for renters at 50+ unit properties, that jumps to 53%) Market insights: 44% Help deciding whether to rent or buy: 37% Negotiating on their behalf: 28% (37% for renters at 50+ unit properties) Zillow AI mode data shows today’s prospective renters are asking about cost early in the process. “Pricing and fees” is the third-most-common search topic in AI mode, following location and amenities. Renters want to know more than the advertised “monthly rent.” They expect to see information about fees, utilities, required deposits, parking, internet access, and other recurring expenses. Clear, consistent cost information across listings is essential for operators that want to stay competitive in the new world of AI-enabled property search. Property comparisons account for 40% of recent renter prompts in Zillow’s AI mode. That’s evidence renters are turning to AI to answer a question listings too often leave unresolved: Which home is right for me, and what will it actually cost to live there? What this means for operators AI is a new path to discovery and consideration. The more detailed the listing, especially in how it anticipates prospects’ affordability concerns, the more likely it is to be found by AI and influence renters’ decisions. To ensure property listings include the affordability information that renters want and that AI tools will look for, operators should: Show the full required monthly cost upfront. Clearly separate mandatory charges from optional add-ons and one-time fees. Keep cost information consistent wherever a property is listed. “Renters cite evaluating and comparing properties as their biggest pain point nearly twice as often as they do finding listings,” Miller says. “Hidden fees, inconsistent pricing, and missing amenity details make it harder to compare, undermining trust and making it harder for renters to confidently choose their property.” Get the full picture of today’s renter AI lets prospects compare already available information about a property. But it can’t fill the information gaps operators leave. By publishing clear, detailed, and consistent information about all costs associated with a property on every platform it’s advertised, operators can ensure their properties show up where renters are looking — and with the right information to answer questions and move renters forward in their consideration. items.title: Nearly Two-Thirds of Phoenix-Area Residents Have Considered Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
items.description:
Nearly Two-Thirds of Phoenix-Area Residents Have Considered
      Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
       New survey finds widespread concern about affordability and support for
         expanding single-family rental housing for Phoenix-area residents

PHOENIX – November 17, 2026 – Nearly two-thirds of Phoenix-area residents have considered moving
because of housing costs, and 91% say housing affordability is a serious problem, according to a new
survey of Phoenix-area residents. Yet most are unaware that Congress recently passed federal
legislation, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, to address affordability concerns.

The survey also found support for expanding access to single-family housing, including newly built rental
homes. Among the key findings:

   ●   Affordability pressures are widespread: Over 91% of Phoenix-area residents say housing
       affordability is a serious problem, and 65% have considered moving because of housing costs.
   ●   Residents want housing choices, including access to single-family homes: 68% believe
       people should have access to single-family homes whether they rent or own, compared to those
       who believe they should only be available to people to own.
   ●   A majority of residents support new rental housing: 55% of Phoenix residents support
       building more rental homes, nearly 2-to-1 over those opposed.
   ●   Renters are feeling affordability pressures: 77% have considered moving because of housing
       costs.


“Housing affordability challenges are affecting communities across the country, and these results
underscore the need for more housing options. No single housing type will solve today’s housing
shortage. We need more opportunities for homeownership, more rental choices, and a continued focus
on expanding supply so families can find housing that meets their needs,” said Adrianne Todman, CEO
of the National Rental Home Council and former Acting Secretary of the U.S. Department of Housing and
Urban Development during the Biden Administration.

The findings come as Arizona policymakers continue to weigh housing affordability, following federal
action this past summer. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act authorized several new programs,
streamlined existing programs, like the HOME grant program, and placed limits on large institutional
investors from purchasing existing single-family homes.

“As state policymakers look ahead to 2027,” Todman said. “the opportunity is to help families find a home
that works for them, close to the jobs and communities they’ve built their lives around.”

About the survey
The survey of 600 Phoenix-area residents was conducted by Pollfish in September 2026.

items.title: The cost of 30 years of certainty
items.description: As mortgage rates top 7%, buyers increasingly turn to adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for monthly savings despite future reset risks. Upfront savings: A 5/1 ARM lowers initial rates by ~1%, saving ~$3,900 annually on a $500,000 loan. Volume surge: ARMs now account for 20% of mortgage dollar volume, led by high-cost states. Strong credit profile: Serious delinquency on post-2010 ARMs sits below 0.5%, proving more resilient than fixed-rate loans There is now a nearly $4,000 annual difference between paying for a $500,000 home with a fixed-rate mortgage and an adjustable-rate mortgage. That figure only grows alongside price. As affordability pushes buyers to make sacrifices, Cotality data shows that there’s been an increase in the number of buyers taking advantage of those extra funds afforded by adjustable-rate mortgages. The savings secured with these flexible mortgages is meaningful, but it’s not stable. “Buyers are taking a bet as affordability wears them down,” said Cotality Principal Economist Archana Pradhan, “They’re choosing available cash in the short term over a guarantee of consistent payments down the road. That solution has very market-dependent results.” An ARM to lean on Conventional wisdom has historically pushed buyers toward adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) when rates are rising. The thinking goes: lock in a rate for 5, 7, or 10 years and then refinance before the mortgage’s fixed period ends. That logic still holds appeal. With current mortgage rates above 7%, people taking out a conventional mortgage today will have a higher rate than most current homeowners; Cotality data shows only 28% of mortgages have interest rates above 5%. Taking out a 5-year ARM at current rates would drop a borrower’s interest rate down around a full point. Accordingly, a full 20% of mortgage dollar volumes are allocated to ARMs, according to Cotality data. However, if the rate adjusts upward following a fixed period, it can quickly eat away at earlier savings. And that reality is a distinct possibility. Cotality economists anticipate that current rates reflect a new normal rather than an anomaly. “Since the 2010s, rates have hovered around 2 to 5 basis points below where they are today. And then pandemic-era rates reset expectations to unrealistic levels,” said Pradhan. “People taking out ARMs today shouldn’t expect the rock-bottom-rates of 2020-2022 when they refinance down the road.” A refinance at the wrong time risks leaving someone exposed to larger monthly payments — and possible default. Buyers are taking a bet as affordability wears them down. They’re choosing available cash in the short term over a guarantee of consistent payments down the road. That solution has very market-dependent results. Archana Pradhan Cotality Principal Economist The price of popularity Affordability is pushing many buyers to the edge. Cotality tracks how homebuyers feel about price pressures , and in a recent survey , 69% of buyers said they were willing to cut lifestyle spending to afford a home. Sixty-five percent seek smaller mortgages for lower monthly payments. Buyers’ eagerness to take on ARMs underscores how strained they are; a few hundred dollars can make the difference between ending the month in the black or the red. Should an adjustable rate mortgage term come up for renewal, current rates could tip monthly payments past the point where homeowners’ finances can absorb the increase. However, Cotality data shows that ARMs are not any more prone to mortgage delinquencies than conventional mortgages. Adjustable-rate mortgages originated after 2010 have a strong track record. Only 0.5% of ARMs from this category are seriously delinquent (90 days or more late), which is slightly lower than fixed rate loans. Even during the economic disruption of early 2020, adjustable mortgages saw serious delinquencies top out at 3.0% as compared to around 3.5% for fixed-rate loans. That’s because households rarely let the mortgage go at the first sign of trouble. Instead, they find room elsewhere in the budget, a trend recorded in Cotality survey data. Sixty-five percent of homebuyers will take out a smaller mortgage to lower monthly payments. For the Gen Z buyers, that figure is 82%. But a smaller mortgage isn’t always possible. In high-cost areas like Washington State, California, and New York, average home prices are $255,000, $324,000, $269,000 above the national average, according to Cotality data. Transactions haven’t slowed, buyers have just become increasingly dependent on ARM loans.
